title: Reading: Unseen and Case-based Passages
short: Discursive and factual passages, MCQ-based, with a speed strategy.
lede: The first section of the paper. It is a speed skill, not a knowledge skill — so practise it daily, not before the exam.
lens: **About 15 marks.** Two passages: a **discursive passage of 400–450 words** and a **case-based factual passage of 200–250 words** with visual input such as statistical data or a chart.
All questions are **objective type**, testing inference, analysis, interpretation, evaluation and vocabulary.
concepts: **1. What is tested.** The questions test **inference** (what is implied but not stated), **analysis** (how an argument is built), **interpretation** (what a word or phrase means in context), **evaluation** (whether a claim is supported), and **vocabulary**. Because the questions are multiple choice, the answer is always in the passage — never bring in outside knowledge.

**2. The method.** (1) Read the **questions first**, quickly, so you know what to look for. (2) Read the passage once at speed for the main idea. (3) Go question by question and locate the line; underline it. (4) Eliminate two options that are clearly wrong, then choose between the remaining two by going back to the text. (5) Do not spend more than ninety seconds on any one question — mark it and return.

**3. Case-based passages.** These come with a chart, graph, table or advertisement. Read the **title, the axes, the units and the scale** before you read the questions. Almost every factual question can be answered from the visual itself, and one question usually asks you to compare two data points.

**4. Vocabulary in context.** When asked what a word means, do not choose the meaning you know from elsewhere. Find the sentence, cover the word, and ask what word would fit. Then check the options against that.
tricks: - **Questions first, then passage.** It saves two or three minutes on a fifteen-mark section.
- In an MCQ, if two options say opposite things, **the answer is usually one of them**.
- For a chart question, always check the **units and the scale** before choosing a number.
mistakes: - Answering from your own knowledge instead of from the passage.
- Choosing a true statement that does not answer the question asked.
- Spending four minutes on one MCQ and running out of time for the writing section.
- Ignoring the chart and reading only the paragraph.

qa.q: What is the difference between a discursive and a case-based passage?
qa.a: A discursive passage is 400–450 words and argues or discusses an idea, so the questions test inference, interpretation and evaluation. A case-based factual passage is 200–250 words and is supported by visual input such as statistical data or a chart, so the questions test your ability to read the data and connect it to the text.

qa.q: Describe a method for attempting the reading section in the time available.
qa.a: Read the questions first, so that you know what to look for. Then read the passage once quickly for the main idea. Go question by question, locate the relevant line and underline it. Eliminate the two options that are clearly wrong, then choose between the remaining two by returning to the text. Keep to about ninety seconds per question and mark any you cannot decide, returning to them at the end.

qa.q: How should you answer a vocabulary-in-context question?
qa.a: Find the sentence containing the word, cover the word, and decide for yourself what word would fit in its place. Then look at the options and choose the one closest to your own word. Do not choose a meaning you have met elsewhere, because the meaning must fit the sentence in front of you.

qa.q: What is the right way to attempt an unseen passage in the board paper?
a: Read the questions first, so that you know what to look for while reading.
Then read the passage once quickly for the sense and a second time to locate the answers, underlining key words.
Answer in complete sentences and, wherever asked, in your own words; do not copy long phrases from the passage.
Stick to the word limit — usually 30 to 40 words for a two-mark question — and number the answers exactly as the questions are numbered.

qa.q: What is the ‘eliminate two options’ rule, and why does it work in the reading section?
a: In every reading MCQ, two options can usually be ruled out at once — one contradicts the passage and one is not mentioned in it at all.
That leaves a fifty-fifty choice between two close options, which you settle by re-reading the exact lines the question points to.
It works because boards design one distractor as opposite and one as out-of-scope; eliminating both is faster and safer than hunting directly for the answer.

qa.q: How should you answer a case-based factual passage with MCQ and short items?
a: Read the whole case once, including any table, chart or data given with it, before looking at the questions.
For the MCQ, choose the option that is supported by the passage and cannot be contradicted by any line in it; do not bring in outside knowledge.
For short items, write one clear sentence with the fact taken from the passage and the number or unit it gives.
Keep every answer brief and grammatical, and do not repeat the question in the answer.

qa.q: You have ninety seconds per question and a 450-word passage. Plan your time across reading, locating and answering.
a: First minute — read the questions, not the passage, so you know what to hunt for.
Next three to four minutes — one fast read of the passage, underlining names, figures and opinion words.
Then about a minute per question — locate the exact line, eliminate two options, mark the answer, and move on without re-reading the whole passage.

mcq.a: **(a) a chart, table or graph.** The questions test whether you can read data, not just prose.

trend: The pattern is stable: one discursive passage and one case-based passage with visual input, all objective. The skill is speed and elimination, not knowledge.
onepager: - Two passages: discursive 400–450 words; case-based 200–250 words with a chart.

- Method: questions first, one fast read, locate the line, eliminate two options.
task: Set a timer for eighteen minutes and do one unseen passage with eight MCQs. Then repeat the same passage the next day and compare your time. Two weeks of this raises the score more than any amount of reading about technique.
steps: 1. Read the **questions first**, then the passage once for the gist and once with the questions in mind — never the other way round.
2. Underline the **sentences that answer each question** as you read them; this saves a second full read in the exam.
3. Write in **complete sentences and your own words**, unless the question says 'from the passage'; then quote, but only the part you need.
4. Keep inside the **word limit**, and finish with a **title** that covers the whole passage rather than one paragraph.

title: Grammar in Context
short: Tenses, modals, subject-verb agreement, reported speech, determiners.
lede: Grammar is tested inside passages and dialogues, not as isolated rules — so practise in sentences, not in tables.
lens: **About 10 marks**, usually as a gap-filling or editing task set within a short passage or dialogue.
The syllabus topics are **tenses, modals, subject-verb agreement, reported speech and determiners**. Clauses, passive voice and prepositions have been removed.
concepts: **1. Tenses.** The tense must agree with the time marker in the sentence. **Since and for** take the perfect tenses; **yesterday, last year** take the simple past; **now, at present** take the present continuous; **tomorrow, next week** take the future. In a narrative passage, the tense often shifts only when the time shifts — so keep the tense until a new time marker appears.

**2. Modals.** **Can** = ability, **could** = past ability or polite request, **may** = permission or possibility, **might** = weaker possibility, **must** = necessity or strong probability, **should** = advice, **would** = a polite offer or a past habit. In reported speech, *will* becomes *would*, *can* becomes *could*, and *may* becomes *might*.

**3. Subject-verb agreement.** The verb agrees with the **subject, not with the nearest noun**. 'The list of items **is** on the table.' Collective nouns take a singular verb when the group acts as one: 'The team **has** won.' With **either…or / neither…nor**, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. **Each, every, everyone, nobody** take a singular verb.

**4. Reported speech.** Change the tense back one step: present → past, past → past perfect, will → would, can → could. Change the pronouns and the time and place words: *today* → *that day*, *tomorrow* → *the next day*, *here* → *there*, *this* → *that*. For questions, use **asked** and change the word order back to statement form: 'Where are you?' becomes *He asked where I was*. For commands, use **ordered, requested or advised** followed by the infinitive.

**5. Determiners.** **A/an** for a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time; **the** for something already mentioned or unique. **Some** in affirmative sentences, **any** in questions and negatives. **Few/a few** with countable nouns, **little/a little** with uncountable. **Much** with uncountable, **many** with countable. **Each/every** with singular nouns, **all/both** with plural.
tricks: - In a gap-filling passage, **look at the other verbs first** — the tense of the passage is usually consistent.
- For subject-verb agreement, **cross out everything between the subject and the verb** and then decide.
- In reported speech, count **three changes**: tense, pronoun, time/place word. If you have only made one, look again.
mistakes: - Using the simple past with 'since'. *Since* requires a perfect tense.
- Making the verb agree with the nearest noun in 'the list of items are…'.
- Forgetting to change the word order in reported questions.
- Using 'a' before a word beginning with a vowel *letter* rather than a vowel *sound* — it is 'a university', 'an hour'.

qa.q: Fill in the blank: Neither of the two candidates ____ (has/have) replied yet.
qa.a: **has.** 'Neither of' takes a singular verb, because the subject is 'neither', not 'candidates'.

qa.q: Fill in the blank with a suitable modal: You ____ consult a doctor if the cough persists. (can / should / may)
qa.a: **should** — the sentence gives advice, which is the use of 'should'. 'Can' expresses ability and 'may' expresses permission or possibility, neither of which fits.

qa.q: Choose the correct determiner: There isn't ____ milk left in the jug. (some / any / much)
qa.a: **any** — 'any' is used with uncountable nouns in negative sentences; 'some' is used in affirmative sentences.

qa.q: Change into reported speech: 'Where have you kept my files?' she asked the clerk.
qa.a: She asked the clerk where he had kept her files. Note the three changes: the present perfect becomes the past perfect, the question word order becomes statement order, and 'my' becomes 'her'.

qa.q: Fill in the blanks with a reason for each: (i) Slow and steady ___ (win/wins) the race. (ii) No news ___ (is/are) good news.
a: (i) wins — ‘slow and steady’ is a single combined idea (one subject), so the verb is singular.
(ii) is — ‘news’ looks plural but is an uncountable singular noun, so it takes a singular verb.

qa.q: How do you change a sentence from direct into indirect speech?
a: Change the reporting verb into the past tense; since the reporting verb is already in the past, the verb in the reported clause moves one step back — present to past, past to past perfect.
Change the pronouns according to sense, and change words of nearness into words of distance: now becomes then, today that day, tomorrow the next day, here there.
Remove the inverted commas and the comma after the reporting verb, and use ‘if' or ‘whether' for yes–no questions.
Do not change a universal truth: ‘The teacher said that the earth moves round the sun' keeps the present tense.

qa.q: Correct these sentences and give a reason for each: (i) She don't like mangoes. (ii) He is working since morning. (iii) The teacher said that the earth moved round the sun. (iv) Neither of the boys were present.
a: (i) She doesn't like mangoes — a third-person singular subject takes does not, not do not.
(ii) He has been working since morning — an action continuing up to the present uses the present perfect continuous, not the present continuous.
(iii) The teacher said that the earth moves round the sun — a universal truth keeps the present tense even in indirect speech.
(iv) Neither of the boys was present — ‘neither' is singular, so the verb is was, not were.

mcq.a: **(b) was.** ‘Neither' and ‘either' are treated as singular in formal English.

mcq.q: The correct reported form of ‘He said, “I am busy”' is: (a) He said that he was busy  (b) He said that he is busy  (c) He said that I was busy  (d) He says he was busy
mcq.a: **(a) He said that he was busy.** The pronoun changes to he and the tense moves one step back.

mcq.a: **(a) if.** A reported yes/no question joins the main clause with if (or whether), never that.

trend: The topics are fixed — tenses, modals, subject-verb agreement, reported speech and determiners — and are tested inside a passage or dialogue, so the skill is recognising the pattern in context.
onepager: - Tenses follow the time marker; since and for take perfect tenses.
- Modals: can ability, may permission, must necessity, should advice.
- The verb agrees with the subject, not the nearest noun; neither/either take the nearer subject.
- Reported speech: shift tense, change pronoun, change time and place words, and restore statement word order in questions.
- Determiners: some in affirmatives, any in negatives and questions; few with countable, little with uncountable.
task: Take any page of a story book, remove ten function words and verbs at random, and fill them back in from memory. Then check. This is exactly the gap-filling exercise the paper sets, and it trains the pattern recognition the questions need.
steps: 1. Read the **whole sentence** before the blank — the tense, subject and voice are usually fixed by the sentence, not the blank.
2. Name the **choice you are making**: a tense, a modal, a determiner, a preposition or a passive form.
3. Apply the rule and **read the sentence again** with your answer in it; most errors are caught by ear.
4. For narration and voice changes, change **one thing at a time** — pronoun, then tense, then time and place words — and check each.

title: Formal Letter Writing
short: Letters to the editor and letters of order, enquiry, complaint.
lede: Ten marks that depend almost entirely on format and word limit.
lens: **10 marks, 100–120 words.** Two kinds are set: a **letter to the editor** and a **letter of order, enquiry or complaint** to a firm or an official.
**Format marks are awarded separately.** Stick to the word limit.
concepts: **1. The format.** (1) **Sender's address** at the top left, in two or three lines, without the name. (2) **Date**, written in full — 15 March 2027, not 15/3/27. (3) **Receiver's designation and address** — The Editor / The Manager, the name of the newspaper or firm, and the city. (4) **Subject**, in one line, short and specific. (5) **Salutation** — Sir / Madam. (6) **Body** in three short paragraphs. (7) **Complimentary close** — Yours faithfully / Yours sincerely. (8) **Signature, name and designation**, if given.

**2. The three paragraphs.** **First:** state the purpose in one sentence — 'Through the columns of your esteemed daily, I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to…' for a letter to the editor, or 'I wish to place an order for…' for a letter of order. **Second:** give the details — the problem, the specification, the number and model, the complaint, or the data and examples. **Third:** state what you want done, politely and specifically, and end with the expectation of a reply or of action.

**3. Letter to the editor.** The tone is formal and public-spirited; the letter raises a social or civic issue, supports it with two or three concrete details, and ends with a request that the authorities be urged to act. It never names individuals or makes accusations.

**4. Letter of order, enquiry or complaint.** **Order:** give the item, model, quantity, the price quoted, the mode of payment, the delivery date and the address. **Enquiry:** ask specific questions and request a quotation and the terms. **Complaint:** give the invoice number, the date, exactly what is wrong, and the remedy you expect — replacement, refund or repair — with a reasonable deadline.
tricks: - **The subject line is one line only.** If it runs to two, shorten it.
- **'Yours faithfully'** with Sir/Madam; **'Yours sincerely'** only when you use the person's name.
- Keep the body to **three paragraphs of three to four sentences**. The word limit is checked.
mistakes: - Putting your name in the sender's address at the top. It goes at the **bottom**, under the signature.
- Writing the date as 15/3/27. Write it in full.
- Exceeding 120 words — this costs marks even if the content is good.
- Using informal language or contractions such as 'don't' or 'I'm'.

qa.q: Give the format of a formal letter.
qa.a: Sender's address at the top left, without the name; the date in full; the receiver's designation and address; a one-line subject; the salutation Sir or Madam; the body in three short paragraphs; the complimentary close Yours faithfully or Yours sincerely; and the signature, name and designation at the bottom left.

qa.q: What should a letter of complaint contain?
qa.a: It should give the invoice or bill number and the date of purchase, describe precisely what is wrong with the goods or the service, state the remedy required — replacement, repair or refund — and give a reasonable deadline. The tone must be firm but polite, and the letter must end with a request for an early reply.

qa.q: What is the format of a letter to the editor?
a: Sender's address on the left, then the date, then ‘The Editor' with the name of the newspaper and its city.
Then the subject line in brief, then the salutation ‘Sir' or ‘Madam'.
The body: introduce the issue in one sentence, explain the problem and its effect, suggest two or three solutions and end with a hope that the authorities will act.
End with ‘Thanking you' or ‘Yours truly', and then the sender's name and designation or address.

qa.q: What are the three paragraphs of the body of a formal letter expected to do? Illustrate with a complaint about damaged goods.
a: Paragraph 1 states the purpose — the order number, date and the fact that the goods arrived damaged.
Paragraph 2 gives the details — which items are broken, how the packing failed, and what the invoice says.
Paragraph 3 states what you want done — replacement, refund or repair — with a clear, polite deadline.

title: Analytical Paragraph
short: A data-based paragraph from a chart, graph, table or set of clues.
lede: Ten marks for describing data you are given. Nothing has to be invented — the answer is in front of you.
lens: **10 marks, 100–120 words.** Based on a **chart, graph, table, data set, outline or set of clues**.
The marks go to **accurate description, comparison and a concluding inference** — not to opinions.
concepts: **1. The structure.** **First sentence:** introduce the data — what the chart shows, what period it covers and what units are used. **Middle sentences:** describe the main features, comparing and contrasting the significant figures. **Last sentence:** give a conclusion or a trend inferred from the data. Do not list every number — select the two or three that matter.

**2. The language of description.** **Comparison:** higher than, lower than, twice as much as, three times the figure for. **Trend:** rose steadily, fell sharply, remained constant, fluctuated, peaked in, reached a low of. **Proportion:** accounted for, made up, constituted, represented. Use these phrases rather than repeating 'it increased'.

**3. What not to do.** Do not give your opinion or a recommendation unless the question asks for one. Do not invent data that is not in the chart. Do not exceed the word limit. Do not write a story — this is a description, not a narrative.

**4. Worked example.** Given a table showing the percentage of households with internet access in 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2025, a good paragraph would open: *'The table shows the percentage of households with internet access over a fifteen-year period from 2010 to 2025.'* It would then compare the figures, noting the sharpest rise and any period of stagnation, and close with the overall trend and its implication.
tricks: - **Open with what the chart shows, then compare, then conclude.** Three moves, one paragraph.
- **Pick three figures, not ten.** Examiners reward selection, not transcription.
- Learn six comparison phrases and use them. Repeating 'it increased' loses language marks.
mistakes: - Copying every number from the table.
- Adding an opinion or a recommendation that was not asked for.
- Writing 'the chart is very interesting' — description, not comment, is what is rewarded.

qa.q: Describe the structure of an analytical paragraph.
qa.a: The paragraph opens with a sentence introducing the data — what it shows, the period it covers and the units used. The middle sentences describe the main features, selecting the significant figures and comparing them. The final sentence gives a conclusion or a trend inferred from the data. The whole paragraph is within the word limit and contains no opinion.

qa.q: What should an analytical paragraph avoid?
qa.a: It should avoid giving personal opinions or recommendations unless the question asks for them, inventing data that is not in the chart, listing every figure instead of selecting the significant ones, and exceeding the word limit. It should describe and compare the data, not comment on it.

qa.q: What is the structure of an analytical paragraph?
a: Begin by naming the data: what the chart or table shows, over what period and for whom.
Then give the main trend or the largest and smallest categories, using the figures in the data.
Next explain the reasons or the pattern behind the figures, comparing categories where useful.
End with a conclusion or a suggestion, and keep the whole paragraph to about 100 to 120 words.

qa.q: Which phrases of comparison and trend should an analytical paragraph use? Give four examples with the situation for each.

‘Fell sharply’ — for a sudden drop, as in accidents after speed cameras were installed.
‘Peaked in’ — for the highest point, as in sales peaking in December.
‘Twice as much as’ — for direct comparison, as in bus users being twice as many as car users.

qa.q: A survey of 200 students of a school showed these preferences for co-curricular activities: Sports 80, Music 50, Art 40, Debate 30. Write an analytical paragraph.
a: A survey of 200 students shows clear preferences among the four co-curricular activities offered by the school.
Sports is the most popular choice, preferred by 80 students, or 40 per cent of those surveyed, while music is second with 50 students, or 25 per cent.
Art is chosen by 40 students (20 per cent) and debate by only 30 (15 per cent), which together account for just over a third of the students.

The pattern suggests that physical activity attracts the largest number of students, while activities that require performance in front of an audience, such as debate, attract the fewest; the school could encourage the less popular activities by giving them more time, trained coaches and recognition.

qa.q: A student writes: ‘I think the chart is wrong and the school should buy more buses.’ Identify what is wrong with this sentence for an analytical paragraph.
a: First, ‘I think the chart is wrong’ disputes the given data — the data must be accepted and analysed, never challenged.
Second, ‘the school should buy more buses’ is a personal opinion and a suggestion — analytical paragraphs report trends and inferences, not opinions.
The correct close would state what the data shows, for example that bus use dominates and is still rising.

qa.q: Write an analytical paragraph on a bar chart showing the mode of transport used by students: bus 45%, cycle 25%, walk 20%, private car 10%.
a: The bar chart shows how students travel to school, expressed as a percentage of the total number of students.

The most common mode of transport is the bus, used by 45 per cent of students — almost half. Cycling is the second most popular, at 25 per cent, while 20 per cent of students walk to school. Only 10 per cent travel by private car, the least common mode.

Taken together, the figures show that the great majority of students — 90 per cent — use public or non-motorised transport, and that reliance on private cars is minimal. This suggests that improving bus services and cycle lanes would benefit far more students than any measure aimed at car users.

- Close: state the trend or an inference.

task: Find any graph in a newspaper or a textbook and write a 100-word analytical paragraph on it in ten minutes. Then underline your comparison phrases — if you cannot find four, rewrite using more of them.
steps: 1. Note the **data cue** in the question — it will ask you to analyse a chart, a table, a set of facts or a short extract.
2. Open with one sentence that **states what the data shows overall**, not with the numbers themselves.
3. Develop **two or three points** with the figures that support them, and say what they mean rather than repeating them.
4. Close with a **conclusion or trend** — the likely direction, the reason, or the implication — and stay inside the word limit.
